| [NOTE-019](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-019.md) v2 | Reckless disregard for the truth coming from cops, doctors, and scientists | Gelman argues that scientists (a 3-day study titled "long-term"; the power-pose abstract's "instantly become more powerful"), a paid medical expert (Ludmerer's 2002 "no opinion" on smoking and lung cancer) and DHS spokespeople (Lander "assaulting", Padilla "lunging", ICE's unsourced "413 percent" assaults) share one pattern, which he calls "reckless disregard for the truth". | [NOTE-034](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-034.md) v2 | Curry et al. 2019, morality-as-cooperation in 60 societies | Coding 3,460 eHRAF paragraphs on the 60 Probability Sample Files societies found 962 morally valenced mentions of seven cooperative behaviours, 961 of them positive. The one negative is Chuuk admiration of open theft as dominance. Presence varied widely by domain: property 54/60 (90%), kin 47 (78%), group 44 (73%), reciprocity 43 (72%), respect 35 (58%), bravery 32 (53%), fairness 9 (15%). Presence correlated with ethnographic coverage (r = 0.43). The design can detect a morally positive mention but has almost no way to register a negative one, so the 99.9% is weak evidence for universality. | Read |
| [NOTE-093](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-093.md) v2 | Bruckner — Welfare Subjects and Autopoiesis | Bruckner proposes, by abduction and not deduction (§4), that being autopoietic is sufficient, not necessary, for being a welfare subject. An entity is autopoietic when it "sustains, maintains, and renews itself in a way that responds and adapts to its environmental conditions". On this view insentient plants and a hypothetical non-sentient self-maintaining car ("Tessler") are welfare subjects, while engines with governors, thermostats and heat-seeking missiles are not. He answers the charge of absurd obligations in two ways: welfare value may not generate agent-neutral reasons at all, and if it does, the reasons concerning non-conscious subjects are "extremely weak" (Bradford 2023). | Read |

| [NOTE-144](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-144.md) v2 | Consent and the formation of preferences | Whether consent based on a preference switches the moral facts depends on how the preference was formed, and the criterion is "the space and resources those mechanisms leave for the free exercise of agency" (p. 5, restated p. 9): preferences formed by unjust Sanctions, or by Beliefs formed in an unjustly manipulated evidential environment, diminish consent's effectiveness, while preferences formed by Attention do not, even when an unjust force imposed the contact. | [NOTE-151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-151.md) v2 | Register — The Depth of the Body | Register argues that body parthood "for moral purposes" is bounded below by depth. Depth is the microphysical commitment of an object's real definition, and objects that are "too deep" (a water molecule, the parcel of matter now composing the heart, a particular cloud server) are not body parts, though they are parts in the ordinary sense. His two principles ("bodily interests/rights are high-level") say that events which are high-level neutral do not bear on bodily rights or interests. So a BCI user's implemented software can be a body part owned by the user while the third-party server that runs it is not. | Read |
| [NOTE-156](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-156.md) v2 | Towards ethical evolution: responsible AI autonomy | The paper proposes, without implementation, formalism or experiment, that an AI system which designs further AI systems should pass on one "immutable" principle. The principle is: do not directly harm humanity or violate fundamental human values; monitor and mitigate misuse of your outputs; and make every derivative inherit this principle (p. 12). The mechanisms are a genetic-algorithm analogy, with immutable and mutable "genes", constrained crossover and filtered mutation, together with "temporal cloning". The paper is inconsistent about its central notion. The principle is enforced once by a penalty F = Q − α·P (p. 9) and once by "unbreachable" hard constraints (p. 13). And it is "immutable" only in its architecture, while its ethical content stays "adaptable" (p. 14). | Read |

| [NOTE-181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-181.md) v2 | The Moral Status of Animals (SEP) | The entry reviews five proposed grounds of moral considerability (species membership, human-exceptional capacities, personhood, sentience and agency). Its conclusion is that attempts to establish human uniqueness by capacities are "not the most promising" (§1.2). It then separates *having* moral status from the *weight* of a claim ("showing up on a moral radar screen", §2.2). Weight depends on the value theory adopted for animal interests (hedonism, preference satisfaction, objective list; §2.1) and on the normative framework (rights, which are absolute but generate forward-looking duties when violated, or a multi-factor utilitarianism). It closes with virtue-ethical, feminist, relational and empathy-based approaches that reject argument from capacities altogether (§3). | Read |

| [NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md) | The moral psychology of obligation | Tomasello proposes that the human sense of obligation is "the internalized social/rational pressure from a joint or collective self-regulating agent 'we'… to do what 'we' expect me to" (§3). It arises first, around age 3, inside joint-commitment collaboration with a partner, and then, from about 3–5 years, toward in-group members through collective identification. It is a "self-conscious motivation" whose coercive force is a threat to one's cooperative identity. The support is a synthesis of developmental and comparative experiments, mostly from his own lab, on WEIRD children versus chimpanzees; the paper runs no new experiment. | Read |
